description: Build system, dependency security, per-crate feature gates, and CI workflow completeness.

reviews.title: Workspace Cargo.toml: dependency vulnerabilities, MSRV, feature flags
reviews.prompt: Workspace Cargo.toml defines the shared dependencies and metadata for the entire HARES Rust workspace. Review: (a) Dependency vulnerabilities: identify known CVEs or security advisories for the major dependencies. nalgebra 0.34: check for any linear algebra vulnerabilities (historically nalgebra had unsoundness issues in generic matrix operations). arrow/parquet 58: large data processing library with complex dependencies; check for deserialization vulnerabilities in Parquet file reading. pyo3 0.28: Python-Rust FFI bridge; verify no unsound use of unsafe code that could cause memory corruption when Python objects cross the FFI boundary. quick-xml 0.39: XML parser; check for entity expansion (billion laughs) and recursive XML bombs—if untrusted HPXML files are parsed, these are critical. (b) MSRV 1.87 compatibility: verify all workspace crates compile with the declared MSRV (Minimum Supported Rust Version). Check that no dependency requires a newer Rust version than 1.87—a transitive dependency bumping its MSRV can silently break builds on older toolchains. (c) Feature flag correctness: tracing release_max_level_info must be set in the release profile to strip trace/debug events from release builds. Verify this feature is enabled in the workspace Cargo.toml under [profile.release] or in the tracing dependency features. If missing, debug-level tracing causes significant runtime overhead in release builds. (d) Check for dependency duplication: multiple incompatible versions of the same crate (e.g., serde 1.x and serde 0.9.x) bloat compile times and binary size. Run `cargo tree -d` to identify duplicates. (e) Verify the workspace members list includes all crates under crates/—an unlisted crate won't benefit from workspace-level settings and may use different dependency versions.

reviews.title: Per-crate Cargo.toml: feature flag completeness and dev-dependency leakage
reviews.prompt: Each crate under crates/hares-*/ has its own Cargo.toml. Review all 10+ crates for: (a) Feature flag completeness: every optional feature (e.g., check-invariants, python-bindings, serde-json, graphical-output) must be correctly declared and gated with #[cfg(feature = "...")]. A feature enabled at workspace level but not declared in the crate will silently not compile the gated code. (b) Optional features correctly gated: code behind check-invariants should perform runtime invariant checks (energy balance, non-negative volumes, etc.) that are expensive and should not run in production. Verify this feature adds real runtime checks that are absent without the feature—a common anti-pattern is declaring a feature that changes nothing. (c) Dev-dependencies don't leak into production: dev-dependencies (e.g., proptest, criterion, tempfile) must be under [dev-dependencies], not [dependencies]. A dev-dependency in [dependencies] bloats the final binary and introduces unnecessary attack surface. Verify by inspecting Cargo.toml of each crate for misplaced dev-dependencies. (d) Dependency version consistency: the same dependency across crates (e.g., serde, itertools, anyhow) should use the same version. Version mismatches cause duplicate compilation and subtle type compatibility issues—a type from serde 1.0.210 cannot be used with a function expecting serde 1.0.203. (e) Optional dependencies tied to features correctly: if a config implies "serde_json" is needed for JSON output, the Cargo.toml should have `serde_json = { version = "...", optional = true }` and the feature should enable it. Verify the feature-to-dependency mapping for all optional dependencies. (f) Check for unused dependencies: dependencies listed but never imported waste compile time. Verify each dependency is actually used in the crate's source.

reviews.title: CI workflow matrix: missing test jobs, clippy strictness, benchmark regression
reviews.prompt: The CI workflow currently runs fmt + clippy only. This is severely insufficient for a scientific computing codebase where correctness is paramount. Review for missing jobs and recommend additions: (a) `cargo test` per crate: each crate should have its own test job running `cargo test -p hares-CRATE`. This separates test failures by component and parallelizes CI. Currently, if tests aren't run at all, regressions go undetected. (b) `cargo nextest run`: nextest is faster and produces better test output than cargo test. Consider adopting nextest for CI. (c) Python test suite: the Python companion library in py-companion/ needs its own test runner (e.g., pytest with coverage). Verify the test suite exists and is invoked by CI—if the Python tests exist but aren't in CI, they bitrot. (d) Benchmark regression: if the crate has benchmarks (criterion or iai), CI should run them and compare against previous results to detect performance regressions. A change that makes the thermal solver 10x slower could go undetected without benchmark CI. (e) Stricter clippy: currently clippy is run, but which lint level? Verify it's at least `clippy::all` with `-D warnings` (deny all warnings). Recommend adding: clippy::pedantic (for extra lints), clippy::nursery (experimental lints), rust_2018_idioms, missing_docs (to enforce documentation coverage). (f) Miri (undefined behavior detection): for a crate with unsafe code (pyo3 bindings, SIMD math), CI should run Miri to detect UB. (g) Cross-platform: CI should include multiple targets (at minimum x86_64-linux and aarch64-apple-darwin) since floating-point behavior differs. (h) Vendor CI comparison: OCHRE and EnergyPlus CI workflows in vendors/ have more comprehensive test matrices (EnergyPlus runs ~5000 integration tests). Compare the CI strategy and adopt any gaps. (i) Code coverage: add cargo-tarpaulin or cargo-llvm-cov to track and gate code coverage.
